claim: NMDA receptor (NMDAR)-dependent forms of synaptic plasticity are thought to underlie the assembly of developing neuronal circuits.
source: NMDA receptor (NMDAR)-dependent forms of synaptic plasticity are thought to underlie the assembly of developing neuronal circuits and to play a crucial role in learning and memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific consensus about NMDAR function in neural development.

claim: NMDAR plays a crucial role in learning and memory.
source: NMDA receptor (NMDAR)-dependent forms of synaptic plasticity are thought to underlie the assembly of developing neuronal circuits and to play a crucial role in learning and memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific consensus about NMDAR function.

claim: Nascent granule cells lacking NMDARs but rescued from apoptosis by overexpressing Bcl2 were deficient in spine formation.
source: Here we demonstrate that nascent GCs lacking NMDARs but rescued from apoptosis by overexpressing the pro-survival protein Bcl2 were deficient in spine formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 3.

claim: Insufficient spinogenesis might be a general cause of cell death restricted within the NMDAR-dependent critical time window for GC survival.
source: Insufficient spinogenesis might be a general cause of cell death restricted within the NMDAR-dependent critical time window for GC survival.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental observations about spine formation deficiency in Bcl2-rescued cells.

claim: NMDAR loss led to enhanced mushroom spine formation throughout the development of newborn GCs.
source: NMDAR loss also led to enhanced mushroom spine formation and synaptic AMPAR activity throughout the development of newborn GCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1, 4, and 5.

claim: NMDAR loss led to enhanced synaptic AMPAR activity throughout the development of newborn GCs.
source: NMDAR loss also led to enhanced mushroom spine formation and synaptic AMPAR activity throughout the development of newborn GCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figures 1J-L.

claim: Similar elevated synapse maturation in the absence of NMDARs was observed in neonate-generated GCs.
source: Moreover, similar elevated synapse maturation in the absence of NMDARs was observed in neonate-generated GCs and CA1 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Similar elevated synapse maturation in the absence of NMDARs was observed in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: Moreover, similar elevated synapse maturation in the absence of NMDARs was observed in neonate-generated GCs and CA1 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: NMDAR operates as a molecular monitor for controlling the activity-dependent establishment and maturation rate of synaptic connections between newborn neurons and others.
source: Together, these data suggest that NMDAR operates as a molecular monitor for controlling the activity-dependent establishment and maturation rate of synaptic connections between newborn neurons and others.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental observations throughout the study.

claim: New neurons are continuously generated in the hippocampus of the adult mammalian brain.
source: New neurons are continuously generated in the hippocampus of the adult mammalian brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about adult neurogenesis.

claim: New neurons become granule cells (GCs), the principal neurons in the dentate gyrus (DG) of the hippocampus.
source: These neurons become granule cells (GCs), the principal neurons in the dentate gyrus (DG) of the hippocampus, and they functionally integrate into the hippocampal circuitry (van Praag et al., 2002; Toni et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: New neurons functionally integrate into the hippocampal circuitry.
source: These neurons become granule cells (GCs), the principal neurons in the dentate gyrus (DG) of the hippocampus, and they functionally integrate into the hippocampal circuitry (van Praag et al., 2002; Toni et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Structural remodeling in adult neurogenesis requires activation of NMDA receptors (NMDARs).
source: This extreme form of structural remodeling, similar to many other forms of experience-dependent plasticity, requires activation of NMDA receptors (NMDARs) (Platel and Kelsch, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Blockade of NMDARs rapidly increases the proliferation of neural precursor cells.
source: Blockade of NMDARs rapidly increases the proliferation of neural precursor cells, whereas stimulation of NMDARs promotes neuronal fate specification (Cameron et al., 1995; Deisseroth et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Stimulation of NMDARs promotes neuronal fate specification.
source: Blockade of NMDARs rapidly increases the proliferation of neural precursor cells, whereas stimulation of NMDARs promotes neuronal fate specification (Cameron et al., 1995; Deisseroth et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Deletion of the NMDAR subunit NR1 reduces the survival rate of adult-born GCs.
source: Moreover, deletion of the NMDAR subunit NR1 reduces the survival rate of adult-born GCs (Tashiro et al., 2006a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: NMDAR has been primarily known for its involvement in synapse organization and synaptic plasticity.
source: Other than these studies, the role of NMDAR in circuit assembly during new neuron development has so far received little attention, even though NMDAR has been primarily known for its involvement in synapse organization and synaptic plasticity (Constantine-Paton, 1990; Malenka and Nicoll, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and established knowledge.

claim: In newborn GCs, dendritic spines first appear around 16 days after neuronal birth.
source: In newborn GCs, dendritic spines first appear around 16 days after neuronal birth.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research (Zhao et al., 2006).

claim: The spine density increases sharply before cells reach 4 weeks of age.
source: The spine density increases sharply before cells reach 4 weeks of age and continues to increase at a slower pace until reaching a plateau at 8 weeks (Zhao et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Spine density continues to increase at a slower pace until reaching a plateau at 8 weeks.
source: The spine density increases sharply before cells reach 4 weeks of age and continues to increase at a slower pace until reaching a plateau at 8 weeks (Zhao et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The NMDAR-dependent survival/death of adult-born GCs is restricted to the time window of 2–3 weeks after neuronal birth.
source: Notably, the NMDAR-dependent survival/death of adult-born GCs is restricted to the time window of 2–3 weeks after neuronal birth, shortly after formation of the first dendritic spines (Tashiro et al., 2006a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The NMDAR-dependent survival/death of adult-born GCs occurs shortly after formation of the first dendritic spines.
source: Notably, the NMDAR-dependent survival/death of adult-born GCs is restricted to the time window of 2–3 weeks after neuronal birth, shortly after formation of the first dendritic spines (Tashiro et al., 2006a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The survival of newborn GCs may be related to the state of spinogenesis or synaptogenesis.
source: This temporal overlap suggests that the survival of newborn GCs may be related to the state of spinogenesis or synaptogenesis.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the temporal correlation between spine formation and cell survival.

claim: Cell death can be induced by non-innervation at the peak of synaptogenesis during embryonic and postnatal development.
source: Indeed, cell death can be induced by non-innervation at the peak of synaptogenesis during embryonic and postnatal development (Naruse and Keino, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Activation of NMDARs has been shown to support new spine formation.
source: Since activation of NMDARs has been shown to support new spine formation (Maletic-Savatic et al., 1999; Kwon and Sabatini, 2011), we hypothesize that NMDAR is required for initial spine gain on dendrites of newborn GCs and that insufficient spine growth may be the underlying cause of the cell death associated with the genetic deletion of the NMDAR subunit NR1 in newborn GCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is a positive correlation between spine volume and the number of AMPA receptors (AMPARs).
source: There is a positive correlation between spine volume and the number of AMPA (α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole propionic acid) receptors (AMPARs) or, more generally, the synaptic strength (Matsuzaki et al., 2001), supporting the model that spine outgrowth and enlargement are tightly coupled to the formation and maturation of glutamatergic synapses (Zito et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: There is a positive correlation between spine volume and synaptic strength.
source: There is a positive correlation between spine volume and the number of AMPA (α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole propionic acid) receptors (AMPARs) or, more generally, the synaptic strength (Matsuzaki et al., 2001), supporting the model that spine outgrowth and enlargement are tightly coupled to the formation and maturation of glutamatergic synapses (Zito et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Spine outgrowth and enlargement are tightly coupled to the formation and maturation of glutamatergic synapses.
source: There is a positive correlation between spine volume and the number of AMPA (α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole propionic acid) receptors (AMPARs) or, more generally, the synaptic strength (Matsuzaki et al., 2001), supporting the model that spine outgrowth and enlargement are tightly coupled to the formation and maturation of glutamatergic synapses (Zito et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Long-term potentiation (LTP) at mature synapses is associated with NMDAR-dependent enlargement of dendritic spines.
source: Long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD) at mature synapses, expressed by synaptic insertion and removal of AMPARs, respectively, are associated with NMDAR-dependent enlargement and shrinkage of dendritic spines (Yuste and Bonhoeffer, 2001; Matsuzaki et al., 2004; Zhou et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Long-term depression (LTD) at mature synapses is associated with NMDAR-dependent shrinkage of dendritic spines.
source: Long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD) at mature synapses, expressed by synaptic insertion and removal of AMPARs, respectively, are associated with NMDAR-dependent enlargement and shrinkage of dendritic spines (Yuste and Bonhoeffer, 2001; Matsuzaki et al., 2004; Zhou et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Stimuli that induce LTP or LTD may result in rapid outgrowth or loss of spines.
source: Stimuli that induce LTP or LTD may also result in rapid outgrowth or loss of spines, and these changes can be prevented by NMDAR blockers (Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Toni et al., 1999; Nagerl et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Changes in spine outgrowth or loss induced by LTP or LTD stimuli can be prevented by NMDAR blockers.
source: Stimuli that induce LTP or LTD may also result in rapid outgrowth or loss of spines, and these changes can be prevented by NMDAR blockers (Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Toni et al., 1999; Nagerl et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: During early postnatal development, AMPARs can be delivered to spines independently of NMDAR signaling.
source: In contrast, emerging evidence suggests that, during early postnatal development, AMPARs can be delivered to spines independently of NMDAR signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Ultanir et al., 2007; Adesnik et al., 2008; Gray et al., 2011).

claim: NMDARs restrict AMPAR trafficking to the postsynaptic density during early postnatal development.
source: NMDARs actually restrict AMPAR trafficking to the postsynaptic density and limit synapse maturation (Ultanir et al., 2007; Adesnik et al., 2008; Gray et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NMDARs limit synapse maturation during early postnatal development.
source: NMDARs actually restrict AMPAR trafficking to the postsynaptic density and limit synapse maturation (Ultanir et al., 2007; Adesnik et al., 2008; Gray et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Adult-born neurons undergo a long process of maturation resembling embryonic development.
source: Adult-born neurons undergo a long process of maturation resembling embryonic development (Esposito et al., 2005); however, adult neurogenesis happens in mature circuits that differ substantially from the developing brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Adult neurogenesis happens in mature circuits that differ substantially from the developing brain.
source: Adult-born neurons undergo a long process of maturation resembling embryonic development (Esposito et al., 2005); however, adult neurogenesis happens in mature circuits that differ substantially from the developing brain.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the differences between adult and developing brain environments.

claim: rv GFP-ires-cre induced recombination in 97% of GFP+ cells at 6 days post infection (dpi).
source: When tested in the ROSA-lacZ reporter mice, rv GFP-ires-cre induced recombination in 97% of GFP+ cells at 6 days post infection (dpi) and in all GFP+ cells at 14 and 28 dpi.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from testing the retrovirus in reporter mice.

claim: rv GFP-ires-cre induced recombination in all GFP+ cells at 14 and 28 dpi.
source: When tested in the ROSA-lacZ reporter mice, rv GFP-ires-cre induced recombination in 97% of GFP+ cells at 6 days post infection (dpi) and in all GFP+ cells at 14 and 28 dpi.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from testing the retrovirus in reporter mice.

claim: In control adult-born GCs (mcherry+GFP−) at 28 dpi, both AMPA and NMDA currents could be readily evoked by perforant path stimulation.
source: In control adult-born GCs (mcherry+GFP−) at 28 dpi, both AMPA and NMDA currents could be readily evoked by perforant path stimulation (Figure 1B).

claim: In age-matched GFP+ neurons infected by rv GFP-ires-cre, there was only a DNQX-sensitive AMPA component.
source: In contrast, there was only a DNQX-sensitive AMPA component in age-matched GFP+ neurons infected by rv GFP-ires-cre (Figure 1B), suggesting that Cre-mediated recombination successfully removed the floxed Grin1 gene fragment from the mouse genomic DNA.

claim: Cre-mediated recombination successfully removed the floxed Grin1 gene fragment from the mouse genomic DNA.
source: In contrast, there was only a DNQX-sensitive AMPA component in age-matched GFP+ neurons infected by rv GFP-ires-cre (Figure 1B), suggesting that Cre-mediated recombination successfully removed the floxed Grin1 gene fragment from the mouse genomic DNA.

claim: There was no obvious difference in overall cell morphology between NR1 KO and WT cells.
source: There was no obvious difference in overall cell morphology between NR1 KO and WT cells (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: WT and KO cells were similar in both dendritic length (WT: 601.8 ± 36.6, n = 47 frames, KO: 515.1 ± 29.3, n = 38 frames, p = 0.08).
source: Dendritic tracing with the ICL TRACE (http://synapses.clm.utexas.edu/tools/trace/trace.stm) showed that WT and KO cells were similar in both dendritic length (WT: 601.8 ± 36.6, n = 47 frames, KO: 515.1 ± 29.3, n = 38 frames, p = 0.08) and branching points (WT: 5.92 ± 0.33, KO: 5.68 ± 0.37, p = 0.64).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative morphological data.

claim: WT and KO cells were similar in branching points (WT: 5.92 ± 0.33, KO: 5.68 ± 0.37, p = 0.64).
source: Dendritic tracing with the ICL TRACE (http://synapses.clm.utexas.edu/tools/trace/trace.stm) showed that WT and KO cells were similar in both dendritic length (WT: 601.8 ± 36.6, n = 47 frames, KO: 515.1 ± 29.3, n = 38 frames, p = 0.08) and branching points (WT: 5.92 ± 0.33, KO: 5.68 ± 0.37, p = 0.64).

claim: Gross development of dendrites does not require NMDARs.
source: These data indicate that gross development of dendrites does not require NMDARs.

claim: Total spine density was significantly decreased in NR1 KO cells (WT: 2.14 ± 0.08, n = 59 frames, KO: 1.53 ± 0.09, n = 37 frames, p < 0.0001).
source: As shown in Figure 1F, total spine density was significantly decreased in NR1 KO cells (WT: 2.14 ± 0.08, n = 59 frames, KO: 1.53 ± 0.09, n = 37 frames, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative spine density data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The percentage of mushroom type spines relative to total spine numbers was drastically enhanced in NR1 KO cells (p < 0.0001).
source: Surprisingly, the percentage of mushroom type relative to total spine numbers was drastically enhanced, whereas the other spine types remained unchanged (p < 0.0001; Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative spine classification data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Mushroom spine density was increased by more than twofold in NR1 KO cells (WT: 0.026 ± 0.004, KO: 0.064 ± 0.010, p = 0.0001).

claim: The spine head area in NR1 KO cells was bigger than that in control cells (p < 0.0001, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test).
source: A cumulative probability graph of the size of all measured spines showed that the spine head area in NR1 KO cells was bigger than that in control cells (p < 0.0001, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test; Figure 1I).

claim: Both the amplitude and frequency of mEPSCs were significantly increased in neurons lacking NR1 as compared to control cells (WT: n = 5 cells, KO: n = 6 cells, p < 0.001, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test).
source: Both the amplitude and frequency of mEPSCs were significantly increased in neurons lacking NR1 as compared to control cells (WT: n = 5 cells, KO: n = 6 cells, p < 0.001, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test; Figure 1K,L).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 1K and 1L.

claim: NR1 KO cells had enhanced functional glutamatergic synapses.
source: These data confirmed that NR1 KO cells had enhanced functional glutamatergic synapses.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the increased mEPSC amplitude and frequency data.

claim: GFP+ dendritic spines were associated with GFP− axon terminals containing presynaptic vesicles.
source: Utilizing serial immuno-electron microscopy for GFP, we consistently observed that GFP+ dendritic spines were associated with GFP− axon terminals containing presynaptic vesicles (Figure 2A), verifying that newborn NR1-null GCs could form normal synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Newborn NR1-null GCs could form normal synapses.
source: Utilizing serial immuno-electron microscopy for GFP, we consistently observed that GFP+ dendritic spines were associated with GFP− axon terminals containing presynaptic vesicles (Figure 2A), verifying that newborn NR1-null GCs could form normal synapses.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the electron microscopy observations showing proper synaptic structures.

claim: All stubby, thin and mushroom spines were asymmetric and presumably excitatory.
source: We also noted that all stubby, thin and mushroom spines were asymmetric and presumably excitatory (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy observations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Total head volumes of randomly selected spines averaged 0.035 ± 0.005 µm3 (n = 130 spines) in WT GCs and 0.078 ± 0.014 µm3 (n = 74 spines) in NR1 KO GCs, indicating a significant difference between these two groups (p = 0.0008).
source: Total head volumes of randomly selected spines averaged 0.035 ± 0.005 µm3 (n = 130 spines) and 0.078 ± 0.014 µm3 (n = 74 spines) in WT and NR1 KO GCs, respectively, indicating a significant difference between these two groups (p = 0.0008; Figure 2B).

claim: The difference in spine head volume was mainly due to increased volume of big or mushroom spines in NR1 KO neurons.
source: Furthermore, we found that this difference was mainly due to increased volume of big or mushroom spines in NR1 KO neurons, whereas the volumes of small spines (presumably filopodia or thin) were roughly the same across groups.

claim: The volumes of small spines (presumably filopodia or thin) were roughly the same across WT and NR1 KO groups.

claim: Within 28 dpi of rv CAG-GFP, there was a significant decrease in the quantity of GFP+ GCs in C57Bl/6 mice (GFP, relative cell number to that of 14 dpi, 14 dpi: 1.00 ± 0.11, n = 5 mice, 28 dpi: 0.30 ± 0.22, n = 4 mice, p = 0.019).
source: In line with prior studies (Dayer et al., 2003; Tashiro et al., 2006b), within 28 dpi of rv CAG-GFP, we found a significant decrease in the quantity of GFP+ GCs in C57Bl/6 mice (GFP, relative cell number to that of 14 dpi, 14 dpi: 1.00 ± 0.11, n = 5 mice, 28 dpi: 0.30 ± 0.22, n = 4 mice, p = 0.019; Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell quantification data shown in Figure 3A and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: GCs infected by rv GFPBcl2-ires-cre did not die (GFPBcl2icre, 14 dpi: 1.00 ± 0.29, n = 6 mice, 28 dpi: 1.00 ± 0.14, n = 6 mice).

claim: The expression of Bcl2 prevented the death of NR1 KO cells.
source: More importantly, the dramatic death of new neurons observed in Grin1f/f mice injected with rv GFP-ires-cre was not found in Grin1-floxed animals injected with rv GFPBcl2-ires-cre (GFPicre, 7 dpi: 1.00 ± 0.37, n = 5 mice, 21 dpi: 0.05 ± 0.03, n = 5 mice, p = 0.032; GFPBcl2icre, 7 dpi: 1.00 ± 0.31, n = 5 mice, 21 dpi: 1.31 ± 0.39, n = 5 mice, p = 0.5; Figure 3B), suggesting that the expression of Bcl2 did prevent the death of NR1 KO cells.

source: In C57Bl/6 mice, Bcl2-expressing cells displayed decreased dendritic length (GFP: 378.2 ± 32.0, n = 58 frames, cre: 351.5 ± 45.6, n = 33 frames, Bcl2: 283.8 ± 22.0, n = 93 frames, p = 0.013 Bcl2 vs GFP; Figure 3D).

source: The number of dendritic branching points was not significantly different between the samples (GFP: 5.2 ± 0.3, cre: 4.9 ± 1.5, Bcl2: 4.4 ± 0.2, p = 0.056 Bcl2 vs GFP, Figure 3E).

source: Similarly, in Grin1f/f mice, Bcl2-expressing cells displayed a significant decrease in dendritic length (GFP: 342.4 ± 32.9, n = 55 frames, cre: 302.7 ± 22.8, n = 85 frames, Bcl2: 256.0 ± 18.0, n = 133 frames, p = 0.014 Bcl2 vs GFP; Figure 3F) but not in branching points (GFP: 5.4 ± 0.4, cre: 5.1 ± 0.3, Bcl2: 4.7 ± 0.3, p = 0.14 Bcl2 vs GFP, Figure 3G).

claim: Bcl2 expression promoted survival of a mixed population of nascent GCs, including both WT and NR1 KO cells.
source: Since NR1 KO neurons did not display impairment of dendrite length and complexity (Figure 1C,D), we infer from these data that Bcl2 expression promoted survival of a mixed population of nascent GCs, including both WT and NR1 KO cells.

claim: Bcl2-expressing cells in C57Bl/6 mice had much lower total spine density (GFP: 2.13 ± 0.11, n = 28 frames, cre: 2.22 ± 0.11, n = 17 frames, Bcl2: 1.39 ± 0.14, n = 31 frames, p = 0.0001 Bcl2 vs GFP).

claim: A unique population of dendritic branches with low spine density (<1.5 spines/µm) was identified in the Bcl2-expressing group but not in samples expressing GFP or Cre alone.

claim: WT adult-born GCs selected for death had fewer spines, specifically fewer thin spines (p < 0.05), as compared to those destined for survival.

source: In Grin1f/f mice, deletion of NMDAR in newborn GCs led to a decrease in total spine density, and the spine density was even lower in Bcl2-rescued cells (GFP: 1.96 ± 0.06, n = 68 frames, cre: 1.47 ± 0.11, n = 35 frames, Bcl2: 1.06 ± 0.08, n = 45 frames, p = 0.0054 cre vs Bcl2; Figure 3M,N), whereas the cumulative distribution of total spine density did not exhibit significant differences between each pair (p > 0.09, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test; Figure 3O).

claim: Bcl2-rescued group displayed a strong trend of mushroom spine enhancement in Grin1f/f mice (Bcl2 vs GFP: p = 0.08).

claim: NR1 KO GCs accounted for a portion of neurons rescued by Bcl2 and they had more mushroom spines than those dying of reasons other than genetic ablation of NMDARs.
source: However, Bcl2-rescued group displayed a strong trend of mushroom spine enhancement in Grin1f/f mice (Bcl2 vs GFP: p = 0.08, Figure 3Q), but not in WT mice (Bcl2 vs GFP: p = 0.5, Figure 3L), suggesting that NR1 KO GCs accounted for a portion of neurons rescued by Bcl2 and they had more mushroom spines than those dying of reasons other than genetic ablation of NMDARs.

claim: NMDAR was critical for spine outgrowth.
source: Taken together, these data support that NMDAR was critical for spine outgrowth and that newborn GCs destined to die without the protection of Bcl2 were defective in spine formation.

claim: NMDAR activity was required for initial spinogenesis.
source: Using retro- and lentiviral vectors that encode the Cre recombinase, we deleted the Grin1 gene in newborn GCs or mature neurons (GCs and CA1 pyramidal cells) to examine the impact of NMDAR loss on spine morphology. We found that NMDAR activity was required for initial spinogenesis and that a low level of spine density correlated with a defect in cell survival during the 3–4 weeks after new GCs were born, although NMDAR signaling did not appear to have a major impact on total spine numbers in mature neurons, whether they were neonate- or adult-generated.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined experimental data showing decreased spine density in immature NR1 KO cells.

claim: A low level of spine density correlated with a defect in cell survival during the 3–4 weeks after new GCs were born.

We found that NMDAR activity was required for initial spinogenesis and that a low level of spine density correlated with a defect in cell survival during the 3–4 weeks after new GCs were born, although NMDAR signaling did not appear to have a major impact on total spine numbers in mature neurons, whether they were neonate- or adult-generated.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between spine density deficits and cell death in NR1 KO cells.

claim: NMDARs restrict synapse maturation and control spine morphology after spines have been formed, independently of the developmental stage.

claim: The failure of synapse formation may be the underlying mechanism of cell death in NMDAR KO newborn GCs.
source: Through detailed analyses, we found that NMDAR KO newborn GCs that were forced to survive with the expression of the pro-survival gene Bcl2 had defects in spine growth and synaptogenesis. Because the time window of initial spine growth and synapse formation correlated with that of NMDAR-dependent cell survival, we deduced from these observations that the failure of synapse formation may be the underlying mechanism of cell death in NMDAR KO newborn GCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between spine formation deficits and cell death timing.

claim: Natural death of WT adult-born GCs might be a result of the failure of spine formation in certain cell populations.
source: In addition, we analyzed newborn GCs forced to survive through Bcl2 expression in WT mice and found that the overall population had lower total spine density compared to the cells that were selected to survive under natural conditions. This finding suggests that natural death of WT adult-born GCs might also be a result of the failure of spine formation in certain cell populations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the spine density data in Bcl2-rescued WT cells.

claim: Both voluntary exercise and enriched environment (EE) housing increased cell survival.
source: Both voluntary exercise and enriched environment (EE) housing increased cell survival (van Praag et al., 1999; Tashiro et al., 2007; Muotri et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Increased survival of GCs through physical exercise or EE did not lower the average spine density of newborn GCs.
source: However, unlike the forced survival through Bcl2 expression, increased survival of GCs through physical exercise or EE did not lower the average spine density of newborn GCs (Zhao et al., 2014), suggesting that exercise and EE likely promote cell survival through enhancing spine formation in newborn GCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Exercise and EE likely promote cell survival through enhancing spine formation in newborn GCs.

evidence: This claim is speculative, based on known subunit composition effects.

source: However, the observation that NMDAR KO newborn GCs, irrespective of their age, displayed higher mushroom spine density and more synaptic AMPAR activity was unexpected. evidence: This claim is a hypothesis proposed to reconcile conflicting observations.

source: Although the current study has been mainly focused on newborn neurons in the adult brain, our findings suggest that the major neuronal activity detector, NMDAR, regulates the connectivity of specific neurons by common mechanisms in developing and mature nervous systems, including facilitation of new spine formation and control of the pace of existing spine maturation.
